text: I persuaded Bay Ganyo to take a walk to the opera and get tickets for the evening. They were giving the ballet “Purrenfее” and I don’t remember what else. We passed the Greek café, turned toward Café “Mendl,” where the Bulgarians gather, and made our way to the church of St. Stephen. Here in the square I invited Bay Ganyo to stop by a confectionery, not suspecting that the character of Don Juan could get under Bay Ganyo’s skin. But what wonders civilization does work! I should tell you that I was studying in Vienna at the time; I had gone home for the holidays and was now returning, so on the way to Vienna we became acquainted with Bay Ganyo. I used to go to this confectionery often and knew the cashier very well, a pretty and cheerful girl, cheerful, but well-behaved and not allowing any liberties. And imagine, gentlemen, Bay Ganyo and I go into the confectionery, approach the buffet, the girl greets me cheerfully with a welcome, I reply with some playful courtesies, and I turn back to choose something sweet, and at that moment an indignant shriek deafened the whole establishment...
– What happened, Bay Ganyo, did you do something to her? – I cried out anxiously and angrily.
– I didn’t do anything, brother, what have I done? – replied Bay Ganyo, speaking in a tangled way, with a trembling voice.

The girl, angered to the highest degree, with a flushed face and in a loud voice, told me that Bay Ganyo had insulted her by his actions, had grabbed her, and not only had grabbed her, but had also twisted his hand with clenched teeth. She wanted to call the policeman. A scandal!

– You’d better get out of here quickly, Bay Ganyo; if the police catch you, you’re done for. Go on ahead, I’ll catch up with you — I shouted in feigned indignation, and I almost burst out laughing as I looked at Bay Ganyo’s tragicomic figure.

– What’s she putting on airs for! – said Bay Ganyo bravely as he was leaving. – As if she’s honest? I know these local women. Show her the purse—and suddenly, good morning, but your Bay Ganyo isn’t a fool!...

It was my fate to end the impressions of that day with yet another adventure, whose hero was once again our Bay Ganyo. At the opera, as I told you, they were performing the ballet “Rurpenfee.” We had seats in the stalls. The theater was full. Bay Ganyo’s drab clothes stood out like a contrast against the general dark background of the costumes. The curtain rose. Silence — dead silence. Everyone fixed their eyes on the fantastically decorated stage. I could feel that on my right Bay Ganyo was fidgeting, grunting, but I could not tear my eyes away from the stage: the scenes of the ballet kept changing with the movement of a magic wand, various groups of ballerinas appearing and disappearing; on the stage now darkness, now monochrome light, now multicolored light — a fairy spectacle! From the general group of ballerinas one detached herself, stepped forward with tiny quick steps to the front of the stage, stopped, sprang up, and floated through the air, supported only on the tip of one foot... At that very moment, behind my back, a hysterical ha-ha-ha-ha! split the air. I turned left — all the rows behind me were giggling and pointing at something on my right. Instantly something bad flashed through my mind. I turned to Bay Ganyo... Good heavens! What do I see! Bay Ganyo had taken off his sleeves and unbuttoned his vest, which was being tightened by the flasks stuffed into his sash: one of the theater attendants had caught him by the sleeve with two fingers and was making very unmistakable signs with his head for him to go outside; Bay Ganyo stared back at him and answered with signs too — as much as to say, “Who do you think you’re scaring?” It was precisely this swaggering moment that drew hysterical laughter from a little girl sitting behind us, and that laughter infected the whole theater. What a scene! And imagine, gentlemen, I look, overwhelmed with shame, toward the boxes — as if someone were pulling me to look — and my eyes meet the eyes of an entire familiar German family, in whose company I had been very well received, and in their eyes I read sincere pity for my desperate situation. And meanwhile Bay Ganyo was tugging energetically at my sleeve:
– Come on, let’s go out, leave those Jews alone — they’ll fall into my hands, wait!...
